title: Universal Protocol for Extraction of Fructooligosaccharides from Agricultural Byproducts
author: Chelliah, Park, et al.
materials: There is an increasing interest in using agricultural byproducts to find renewable and economically functional raw material sources in various application fields. Agricultural byproducts have nutrients that can be utilized to grow microorganisms that can create valuable enzymes, complex polysaccharides, and crude proteins. The following are examples of agricultural byproducts high in sucrose and can be utilized to make FOS. A similar argument might be made for peeled fruit such as mango, orange, pineapple, or some baguettes, as well as sugarcane, agave, corn, coconut, cassava, and any discarded leaves [14]. In this study, banana peel was used. After drying in an oven at 300 g of fresh banana peel, 50 g of banana powder was obtained using a grinder. Then, after degreasing by the Soxhlet method, a sample was obtained, treated with α-amylase and glucoamylase, centrifuged, and an enzyme-treated banana peel sample was obtained. Then, 99% ethanol was added, the precipitate was formed, lyophilized, and finally, about 20 g of a sample was obtained (Fig. 1).Fig. 1High-performance liquid chromatography with Refractive Index Detector (HPLC-RID) chromatogram of a standard fructooligosaccharide (FOS) from chicory root (F8052-Sigma-Aldrich, South Korea) (GF2 identified peek) compared with banana peel oligosaccharide extract (BPOE) [Determination conditions: mobile phase of acetonitrile and water (80:30, v/v), flow rate 1.0 mL/min, column temperature and RID temperature at 30 °C].Fig 1

Traditional approaches are challenging to identify and separate FOSs due to their structural complexity, high polarity, and difficulty of detection. Furthermore, HSCCC separation is difficult because of their high hydrophilicity, which causes the target compounds to remain in the lower phase, even in n-butanol–water solvent systems. To comply with the HSCCC separation standards, a novel method for FOS preparative separation was used, in which the polarities of FOSs were lowered using acetylation. The compounds were then deacetylated, and FOS separation was confirmed (Fig. 3).Fig. 3The acetylated kestose (GF2) was chromatographed using the HSCCC method. The following solvent systems were used: petroleum ether–n-butanol–methanol-water (3:2:1:4, v/v); stationary phase was in the upper phase; mobile phase was in the lower phase; flow rate was 2.0 mL/min; revolution speed was 800 rpm; retention of the stationary phase was 53.0 percent; sample load was 1 g, and ELSD did detection.Fig 3

HPLC-ELSD analyzed the collected fractions of HSCCC. HPLC was applied to analyze the structure of the target compounds; FOS HPLC optimization. The design of the target compound was analyzed using HPLC, and the ELSD detector was chosen because of its excellent sensitivity and quick application time [16]. Samples eluted with solvent in the C18 chromatographic column have low resolution due to the strong polarity of FOS. The Xamide 100A column was chosen over the Inertsil NH2 Capillary Column for its high resolution and quick processing time. Several elution techniques, including isocratic acetonitrile-water and methanol-water elution, were investigated). The target compounds achieved satisfactory separation when the mobile phase comprised acetonitrile: water (80:20, v/v). The evaporating temperature was 80 °C, the Neb temperature was 90 °C, and the gas flow rate was 1.2 SLM. The column temperature was 30 °C; the mobile phase flow rate was 1.0 mL/min, the evaporating temperature was 80 °C, and the Neb temperature was 90 °C. As a result, a total of 24.9 mg of 1-kestose (GF2) compound was obtained from 1 g of sample, and the final fructooligosaccharide was confirmed to be kestose (GF2) as a result of HPLC-ELSD analysis (Fig. 3).

steps.title: Dry and grind banana peel
steps.instruction: Dry 300 g of fresh banana peel in an oven, then grind the dried material with a grinder to obtain approximately 50 g of banana powder.

steps.title: Degrease powder via Soxhlet extraction
steps.instruction: Subject the banana powder to a Soxhlet degreasing procedure (solvent and time as per standard Soxhlet protocol) to remove lipids.

steps.title: Enzymatic hydrolysis with α‑amylase and glucoamylase
steps.instruction: Treat the degreased banana powder with α‑amylase and glucoamylase under appropriate conditions (enzyme type as named; incubation details not specified).

steps.title: Centrifuge enzyme‑treated mixture
steps.instruction: Centrifuge the enzyme‑treated banana peel suspension to separate the solid and liquid phases (centrifuge speed and time not specified).

steps.title: Ethanol precipitation and lyophilization
steps.instruction: Add 99 % ethanol to the supernatant to precipitate oligosaccharides, collect the precipitate, and lyophilize it to obtain roughly 20 g of dried extract.

steps.title: Acetylate fructooligosaccharides for HSCCC
steps.instruction: Perform acetylation of the hydroxyl groups of the extracted fructooligosaccharides (FOS) to lower polarity before preparative HSCCC separation.

steps.title: Perform HSCCC separation of acetylated FOS
steps.instruction: Load 1 g of the acetylated FOS onto an HSCCC system using the solvent system petroleum ether :n‑butanol : methanol : water (3:2:1:4, v/v). Use the upper phase as stationary phase and the lower phase as mobile phase, set flow rate to 2.0 mL/min, revolution speed to 800 rpm, and retain 53.0 % of the stationary phase. Detect fractions with an ELSD detector.

steps.title: Deacetylate collected fractions
steps.instruction: Remove the acetyl protecting groups from the HSCCC‑collected fractions to regenerate native FOS (deacetylation conditions not specified).

steps.title: Analyze purified kestose by HPLC‑ELSD
steps.instruction: Set up an HPLC system with an Xamide 100A column. For the standard, use a mobile phase of acetonitrile : water (80:30, v/v), flow 1.0 mL/min, column and RID temperature 30 °C. For the sample, use acetonitrile : water (80:20, v/v), flow 1.0 mL/min, column temperature 30 °C, evaporating temperature 80 °C, NEB temperature 90 °C, and gas flow 1.2 SLM. Inject the deacetylated sample and detect with an ELSD. Quantify the yield: 24.9 mg of 1‑kestose (GF2) obtained from 1 g of sample.

steps.title: Conduct particle size analysis (optional)
steps.instruction: Measure the particle size of the purified kestose (GF2); the surface‑area‑equivalent particle size is 6.36 µm.

steps.title: Perform scanning electron microscopy (optional)
steps.instruction: Observe the morphology of purified kestose (GF2) by SEM. Note that standard chicory‑derived GF2 particles range 29.84–58.54 µm (with larger aggregates 108.56–124.88 µm), whereas purified GF2 particles range 55.34–96.11 µm and show a round shape with surface aggregation.
